---
title: "Degree-day methods compared on synthetic temperatures"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", echo = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.6, dpi = 96,
                      out.width = "100%")
options(knitr.kable.NA = "-")
season <- read.csv("data/gdd-synthetic-season.csv")
monthly <- read.csv("data/gdd-synthetic-monthly.csv")
sites <- c("coast", "dryland", "valley", "foothills")
method_order <- c("average", "modified_average", "single_triangle",
                  "double_triangle", "single_sine", "double_sine",
                  "hourly_linvill")
method_col <- c(average = "grey45", modified_average = "#8E5BA8",
                single_triangle = "#E8702A", double_triangle = "#F2A766",
                single_sine = "#0B5563", double_sine = "#5DA9C9",
                hourly_linvill = "#2E8B57")
```

> **These temperatures are synthetic.** They are simulated from real monthly
> normals (WorldClim 2.1 at 30 arc-seconds) at four sites in the Maule
> Region, but the daily and hourly values are generated. The experiment
> measures how much error each method adds under known, controlled
> conditions. It does not replace validation against observed station
> records, which is in progress (`vignette("validation")`).

## Question

Most agroclimatic studies do not have hourly temperature. They have daily
extremes from a station, or monthly climatologies such as WorldClim. How much
error does each degree-day method add in each case?

## Design

The script `data-raw/gdd-synthetic/run.R` reproduces every number on this
page (seed 20261119, about 10 seconds).

1. **Sites.** Four WorldClim 2.1 cells in the Maule Region: coast (Chanco
   area, 69 m), coastal dryland (Cauquenes, 157 m), central valley (Talca
   area, 98 m) and Andean foothills (480 m).
2. **Daily extremes.** The monthly normals densified with `pchip_mp`, plus
   day-to-day anomalies (first-order autoregressive, lag-1 correlation 0.7,
   standard deviation 2.8 degrees C for the maximum and 2.0 for the minimum,
   correlated shocks) and a yearly anomaly. 31 years per site.
3. **Hourly "truth".** The Parton & Logan (1981) diurnal model: a sine by day
   with the maximum lagging solar noon, an exponential decay at night towards
   the next minimum, plus autocorrelated hourly noise. This shape is
   deliberately *not* the sine, triangle or Linvill profile assumed by the
   methods under test, so none of them matches the generator by
   construction.
4. **Reference.** Degree-hours / 24 from the hourly series.
5. **Estimates at three levels**, as in `vignette("validation")`:
   * **daily**: the daily minimum and maximum of the hourly series with
     each daily method, and the Linvill hourly reconstruction;
   * **monthly**: each year's monthly means of those extremes, densified
     with `pchip_mp`, then each daily method;
   * **climatology**: the 30-year mean monthly extremes, densified once and
     compared with every year.
6. **Metrics** for the heat season (1 September - 30 April), 30 seasons per
   site: bias, mean absolute error and relative bias.

The simulated monthly means stay within 0.4 degrees C of the WorldClim
normals; the daily maximum occurs around 13:00 and the minimum around 06:00.

## Results: base 10 degrees C

```{r bias-b10, fig.height = 5.2}
plot_bias <- function(base, upper) {
  d <- season[season$base == base & season$upper == upper, ]
  levels_ <- c("daily", "monthly", "climatology")
  op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 9.5, 2.5, 0.6), oma = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  on.exit(par(op))
  lim <- range(d$rel_bias_pct, 0)
  for (lv in levels_) {
    x <- d[d$level == lv, ]
    ms <- rev(method_order[method_order %in% x$method])
    plot(NA, xlim = lim, ylim = c(0.5, length(ms) + 0.5), yaxt = "n",
         xlab = "Relative bias (%)", ylab = "", main = lv)
    abline(v = 0, col = "grey60")
    abline(v = c(-2, 2), col = "grey85", lty = 2)
    axis(2, at = seq_along(ms), labels = ms, las = 1, cex.axis = 0.9)
    for (i in seq_along(ms)) {
      v <- x$rel_bias_pct[x$method == ms[i]]
      points(v, rep(i, length(v)), pch = 19, col = method_col[ms[i]])
      segments(min(v), i, max(v), i, col = method_col[ms[i]])
    }
  }
}
plot_bias(10, "none")
```

Each point is one site; the line spans the four sites. Dashed lines mark
±2 %.

```{r table-b10}
tab <- function(base, upper, level) {
  d <- season[season$base == base & season$upper == upper &
                season$level == level, ]
  w <- reshape(d[, c("site", "method", "rel_bias_pct")], idvar = "method",
               timevar = "site", direction = "wide")
  names(w) <- sub("rel_bias_pct.", "", names(w), fixed = TRUE)
  w <- w[match(method_order[method_order %in% w$method], w$method),
         c("method", sites)]
  w[sites] <- lapply(w[sites], function(v) sprintf("%+.1f", v))
  rownames(w) <- NULL
  knitr::kable(w, caption = sprintf(
    "Relative bias (%%) of the season total, base %s degrees C, %s level.",
    base, level))
}
tab(10, "none", "daily")
tab(10, "none", "monthly")
```

### What the numbers say

* **Daily extremes.** The triangle methods and the Linvill reconstruction stay
  within about 1 %. The sine methods overestimate by about 2 %, because a
  symmetric sine spends as much time near the maximum as near the minimum,
  while real nights are long and cool. The averaging method underestimates by
  2-6 %, most in the foothills, where the minimum is often below the base
  (Jensen's inequality). The **modified average overestimates by 7-11 %**:
  raising the minimum to the base gives the whole cool part of the day the
  base temperature.
* **Monthly means.** Densified monthly values have no day-to-day
  variability, so cool days with the minimum below the base disappear. That
  lowers every estimate and, for the sine methods, happens to offset their
  positive shape bias: they end up within about 1 %. **This is a
  compensation of two errors, not evidence that the sine is the right
  shape**, and it depends on how variable the real weather is.
* **Climatology.** One climatological year compared with 30 different years
  adds interannual variability: the bias is similar to the monthly level,
  but the mean absolute error grows to about 90 degrees C day for every
  method (table below), larger than most differences between methods.

```{r mae}
d <- season[season$base == 10 & season$upper == "none" &
              season$site == "dryland", ]
w <- reshape(d[, c("level", "method", "mae")], idvar = "method",
             timevar = "level", direction = "wide")
names(w) <- sub("mae.", "", names(w), fixed = TRUE)
w <- w[match(method_order[method_order %in% w$method], w$method),
       c("method", "daily", "monthly", "climatology")]
rownames(w) <- NULL
knitr::kable(w, digits = 0, caption = paste(
  "Mean absolute error (degrees C day) of the season total at the dryland",
  "site, base 10 degrees C. Mean season total: about 1495 degrees C day."))
```

## Results: base 5 degrees C

```{r bias-b5, fig.height = 5.2}
plot_bias(5, "none")
```

With a base of 5 degrees C the minimum is rarely below the base and the
daily methods differ little. They overestimate by about 1-1.5 % (up to
2.4 % for the modified average in the foothills), except the Linvill
reconstruction (0.2-0.3 %): with long cool nights the daily
mid-range \((T_{min} + T_{max}) / 2\) is above the true daily mean, and only
an asymmetric diurnal profile corrects it.

## Seasonal pattern

```{r monthly-profile, fig.height = 4.2}
d <- monthly[monthly$base == 10 & monthly$upper == "none" &
               monthly$site == "dryland" & monthly$level == "daily", ]
ms <- method_order[method_order %in% d$method]
mo <- c(9:12, 1:8)
mat <- sapply(ms, function(m) {
  x <- d[d$method == m, ]
  x$bias[match(mo, x$month)]
})
par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1))
matplot(seq_along(mo), mat, type = "b", pch = 19, lty = 1, lwd = 1.5,
        col = method_col[ms], xaxt = "n", xlab = "",
        ylab = "Mean bias (degrees C day per month)")
axis(1, at = seq_along(mo), labels = month.abb[mo])
abline(h = 0, col = "grey60")
legend("topright", legend = ms, col = method_col[ms], pch = 19, lty = 1,
       bty = "n", cex = 0.8, ncol = 2)
```

At the dryland site, with daily extremes and base 10 degrees C, the methods
agree most in midsummer (December-February), when most of the day is above
the base. From March to November the minimum is usually below 10 degrees C
while the maximum is above it, and the methods diverge: the averaging
method underestimates and the modified average overestimates by 20-30
degrees C day per month, while the triangle methods stay within about 7 and the
Linvill reconstruction within 3 degrees C day.

## Practical guidance

* **With daily extremes**, use a triangle method or the hourly
  reconstruction (`gdd_methods = "hourly"` in `thermify()`). Prefer them
  over the simple average when minimum temperatures fall below the base.
* **With monthly climatologies**, the method matters less than the loss of
  day-to-day variability. Report the method used and treat differences of a
  few percent between methods as within the uncertainty.
* **The modified average** reproduces a published convention (for example
  the "86/50" rule for maize). Use it to match that convention, not as an
  estimate of the integrated heat of the day.

## Limitations

* The generator is one plausible climate and diurnal shape. Different
  day-to-day variability, cloudiness or diurnal shapes change the size, and
  possibly the sign, of the compensations described above.
* The daily minimum and maximum come from hourly means, as in many station
  networks; extremes from sub-hourly records are slightly wider.
* Only the horizontal cutoff and an upper threshold of 30 degrees C were
  evaluated; results with upper thresholds are in the data file and are
  similar to those without one at these sites.
* These conclusions must be confirmed with observed hourly records from
  station networks (issue #3).

## Data

The tables behind this page are in `vignettes/articles/data/`
